activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Elias sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse held up a small bandage. It had little bears on it.

"Will the shot hurt?" Elias asked. He looked at his dad. Dad smiled and held his hand.

"Your arm got tight," the nurse said. "Can you make it soft, like a sleepy cat?" Elias took a big breath. He let his arm go loose and soft. The nurse said, "All done!" It was over before he could count to three.

The shot was fast because his arm was soft. His tight arm made it slow. His soft arm made it quick. Elias thought about that all the way to the ice cream shop.

At the shop, Dad got him a strawberry cone. Elias sat at the small table. He wiggled his fingers and looked at his arm. There was the bear bandage.

"Why does my arm have a bandage?" Elias asked. He answered himself. "The nurse put it there. It stays because it is sticky." He tapped it. It stayed on. It stayed because it was sticky.

Dad laughed. "You are a good noticer, Elias." Elias licked his ice cream. Then he asked, "Can cats get shots too?" Dad said, "Yes, cats get shots too. Maybe they make their arms soft as well." Elias took one more big lick and smiled.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Raphael ran into Grandpa's garage. "I want to make a rocket!" he said. Grandpa smiled and got out the paper and glue.

Raphael squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out in a big puddle. It felt cold and squishy on his finger. He stuck the paper fins on the rocket. Then he picked it up to fly it. The fins slid right off! "Oh no!" said Raphael. The paper was all wet and floppy.

"The glue is still wet," said Grandpa. "Wet glue is slippery." Raphael put the rocket down on the table. He watched and waited. He wiggled his toes. He hummed a rocket song. Finally the glue felt dry and sticky. He picked up the rocket and tapped a fin. It stayed on!

"Zoom, zoom!" said Raphael. He flew the rocket all around the kitchen. "My dad will see it tomorrow!" he said. Grandpa laughed. "I think he will love it," said Grandpa. Raphael gave him a big hug. "Thank you, Grandpa," he said. Then he flew the rocket to the moon, twice.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Anthony sat in a big chair at the restaurant. A giant screen glowed on the wall. It showed a big game. Mom, Dad, and Uncle Ben were there too.

The crowd on the screen waved and jumped. Then a player kicked the ball into the net. Everyone in the restaurant jumped up. They made a big noise! Anthony covered his ears. It was very loud.

Anthony watched some more. The players ran and ran. He saw the ball go close to the net again. Uh oh. Anthony put his hands on his ears first. Then the ball went in! The noise came again, loud and happy.

"The noise comes when the ball goes in," Anthony said. "The goal makes them cheer!" Uncle Ben laughed. "You are a smart one, Anthony!" Anthony smiled and clapped. Then he sent a fry flying across the table with his spoon. Dad caught it and ate it. "Another one!" Dad said, opening his mouth.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Willow brought a big red bag to school. Inside were her show-and-tell things. But the bag fell over and everything rolled out on the rug.

"Oh no," said Willow. "My things are all mixed up."

Her teacher knelt down beside her. "Let's look together," she said.

Willow picked up a carrot, an apple, and a banana. She put them in one pile. "These are foods," she said. "We can eat them."

Then she picked up a ball, a teddy bear, and a toy truck. She put them in a second pile. "These are toys," she said. "We play with them."

A small wooden cow lay by her shoe. Willow looked at it. It went in the toys pile too, because it was a toy, not a real animal.

"You learn fast," said her teacher.

Willow smiled. The same red bag held her things again, all neat and sorted. She zipped it up.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Sofia stood on her stool in the kitchen. She wanted to make her own breakfast. "Can I do it today?" she asked. Mama smiled and put the toast on a plate. The toast was still warm. Sofia picked up the butter knife.

She tried to spread the butter. On cold bread, the butter would have torn it. But the warm toast made the butter soft. The butter went on smooth, like paint. "It glides!" said Sofia. "The warm toast makes it soft!" She looked at her bread. The butter made it shiny. It was a real breakfast, made by her.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the big cup in one hand and poured. The milk splashed out. A puddle grew on the table. "Too fast," she said. She put the cup down on the table. She stood still. She paid close attention to the milk. She poured slowly, slowly. This time not one drop spilled.

Sofia took a big bite of toast. "Mama, does the milk pay attention too?" she asked. Mama laughed. "I think it does, when you go slow." Sofia looked at the white color of the milk in her cup. She clapped her hands.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Anthony looked out the window. The sky was dark and white at the same time. Snow was falling on the grass. No school today! Anthony jumped up and down. "Snow day!" he shouted.

Mom helped him get dressed. One hat. Two mittens. Two boots. One big coat. Anthony counted them all. Then he ran outside. The snow went squeak, squeak under his boots. He made a big snowman with a carrot nose.

Anthony wanted to show Dad the snowman. So he brought a snowball inside. He set it on the table. "Look, Dad!" he said. But then they ate lunch. When Anthony came back, the snowball was gone. There was only a wet spot. "The house is warm," Anthony said. "Warm makes snow melt." He said it again, slowly. "Warm makes snow melt!"

Just then the sun came out. It shined through the window. It hit a piece of ice on the porch. A little rainbow danced on the wall. Anthony pointed at it. "One snowball melted," he said. "One rainbow stayed!"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Myles went to Dad's office after school. He wanted to draw a cat for Mom. Dad gave him a tablet.

Myles tapped the small button. The screen stayed dark. He tapped it again. Still dark. Then Dad held Myles' finger on the button. They counted together, "One, two, three." The screen lit up! "You have to hold it," Myles said. He found the drawing app and drew a fat orange cat.

Later Myles got tired. His eyes felt sleepy. He looked out at the busy street below. "Time to put it away," said Dad. Myles pressed the button until the screen went dark. Then he helped Dad fold the soft blanket. "I did it all by myself," Myles said. Dad smiled and gave him a big hug.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Liam was three today. His party was at the big park. There was cake and balloons. There was even a little farm near the pond.

"Look, ducks!" said Liam. He got some bread. He helped feed the ducks. The ducks came close. They ate the bread fast.

Then Mom called, "Cake time!" Everyone sat on the grass. The cake had three candles. The candles were lit. The little flames wiggled.

"Make a wish," said Dad. Liam squeezed his eyes shut. He wished for a red bike. Then he took a big breath. He blew and blew. The candles went out. All three!

"Is my wish true now?" Liam asked.

"Blowing out the candles is the trick," said his big sister, Maya. "You did it all by yourself!"

Maya tried to blow her party horn. It made a silly sound. She laughed and fell over in the grass.

"Happy birthday, Liam!" said Maya, still laughing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Ayla got a drum from the shop. It had a case with a zipper. She pulled the zipper down. Out came two drum sticks.

In the band room, Ayla held the sticks. She tapped the drum. The sound was tiny. "Why is it so small?" she asked. Her teacher said, "Try again. Take your time."

Ayla tapped once more. Still tiny. She looked at her sticks. They were all crooked. She made them straight. She tapped again. Boom! A big sound came out.

"Ooh," said Ayla. "My sticks were crooked. Now they are straight. The sound is big!" She tapped slowly. Boom. Boom. Boom.

"Can I do it again?" she asked. "Yes," said her teacher. Ayla sat tall and tapped. Boom. Boom. The drum sang.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Daniel sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "Where is the sun?" he asked. It was dark now. Mom said, "The sun went to sleep. It will come back tomorrow." Yesterday the sun was up. Today the sun went down. Tomorrow the sun would come back again. One day, then one day, then one day. Daniel counted on his fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. Three fingers!

Daniel pulled his doll close. "Dolly, the sun is lost," he said. Mom smiled. "No, it is not lost. It is sleeping. Later the sky will be light." Daniel watched the dark road. The car lights made big circles. Then the moon came up. Big and white. "Look!" said Daniel. "The moon is awake now!"

Daniel rubbed his eyes. "Why is the moon out?" he asked. He thought and thought. "The moon is out because the sun went down," he said. Mom said, "Yes, that is right!" The car went bump, bump, bump. Daniel held his doll. Soon he would be home. Then he would sleep. Later it would be morning. And tomorrow, the sun would come back. Daniel waved at the moon. "Bye bye, moon. See you tomorrow!"

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Felix wanted a cheese sandwich. Mom put it on the plate. "First, wash your hands," said Mom. Felix looked at his hands. They looked clean. But he had played on the floor. He had petted the dog.

"I wonder if my hands are stinky," said Felix. He sniffed them. "Yes! Stinky dog hands." He ran to the sink. Mom gave him soap. He rubbed the soap all over. Bubbles grew on his fingers.

"Now we wait," said Mom. "We sing the hand song. It is twenty seconds long." They sang together. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Felix kept rubbing while he sang. The bubbles popped one by one.

"Why do we sing?" Felix asked. "The song is twenty seconds," said Mom. "The soap needs time. Twenty seconds makes the germs go away." The song ended. Felix rinsed his hands. The water carried the bubbles down the drain. His hands smelled like apples now. He held them up to Mom's nose.

"Smell!"

"Not stinky anymore," said Mom. Felix sat down and took a big bite of his sandwich.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Chloe wanted to go outside. It was cold. She put her arms in her coat. Then she pulled the zipper. The zipper did not move. Chloe looked down. The zipper ends were apart.

She tried again, slow this time. She put the two ends together. Click. They stuck. She held the bottom with one hand. With her other hand, she pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up to her chin.

"Look, Mommy! I did it!" said Chloe.

Mommy smiled. "Your coat is on. Your zipper is up. Now we can go."

Chloe ran to the door. Outside, the wind was wild. It blew the leaves across the wood pile. Chloe held her coat tight. "My zipper keeps me warm," she said. Then she jumped in a leaf.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ellie went to the pet store with Dad. She saw a small brown hamster. "I want that one," she said. "Can I hold him now?"

Dad shook his head. "New hamsters need to go home first," he said. "Then we wait."

Ellie took the hamster home in a little box. She put him in his cage. She wanted to play. She put her hand in. The hamster ran into his little house and hid.

"Did I do something bad?" Ellie asked.

"You were too fast," said Dad. "He hides because everything is new."

Ellie felt sorry. She sat down on the floor. She did not move. She waited and waited.

The hamster peeked out. He turned his tiny head. He sniffed the air. Then he walked to his food bowl and ate a seed.

Ellie watched him, very still. "I will wait every day," she said. "Then you will like your new playground."

The hamster stuffed one more seed in his cheeks.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Leon had three little paint pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. The blue pot had a picture of waves. Mom said, "This blue is called ocean blue." Leon liked the ocean blue best.

Leon wanted to paint a green frog. But he had no green paint. He looked in his pots. Red, yellow, ocean blue. No green. Leon felt sorry for the frog with no paint. Then Leon had an idea.

He dripped ocean blue into a cup. He dripped yellow in too. He mixed it with his brush. Round and round. The paint turned green! Leon said, "Blue and yellow make green." He said it again. "Blue and yellow make green!"

Leon painted the frog green. Then he washed his brush in the water tub. The brush was heavy with paint. It sank down, down to the bottom. Leon pulled it up and laughed. He held it up to the sun. "My green frog," said Leon. "One, two, green."

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
It was Ellie's birthday. A big paper sign would hang on the wall. Papa held it up high. "I can't reach," said Papa. Ellie got the little chair. Now the sign could hang just right.

The friends came in. Mama put down cupcakes. But one candle was lost! Ellie looked under the table. She found it by the owl toy. The owl was sitting on the candle. "Silly owl," said Ellie. The owl seemed to wink.

Mama said, "How many candles now?" Ellie counted. "One, two, three!" Three candles, because she was three years old. Grandpa blew one out. "Hey!" said Ellie. He laughed. She blew out two. Papa clapped and clapped. Ellie took a big bite of cupcake. Frosting was all over her nose. "One, two, three kisses," said Mama. She counted them out loud.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Lucy went to the park with her red balloon. A little boy sat near the sandbox. His ice cream had fallen in the sand. His eyes were wet. His mouth turned down. He looked sad.

Lucy wanted to help. She held out her balloon. "Do you want to hold it?" she asked. The boy shook his head. He was still sad. Lucy waited. She sat down near him. She waited some more.

Then a big dog ran by, barking loud. The boy grabbed Lucy's hand. His eyes got wide. He was scared. Lucy was scared too. She squeezed his hand softly. They sat very still. The dog ran past. It did not stop. The boy looked at Lucy. "The dog is gone," he said. His mouth turned up a little.

Lucy had an idea. She gave the boy a big hug. She held on and counted, one, two, three. When she let go, the boy was smiling. "Hugs make sad go small," said Lucy. Then the sky changed color. Pink and orange clouds! Both kids pointed up. "Wow!" they said at the very same time.

The boy's mom came back with a new ice cream. He took a bite and laughed. Lucy waved her balloon high. "Best park day," she said.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Everly sat in the big red seat. Grandma had brought her to the concert hall. On the stage, a lady began to play a song. It was "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Everly loved that song.

Everly wanted to clap along. She clapped very fast, clap clap clap clap. But her hands did not match the song. The song went slow, like a walk. Her claps went fast, like a run. "Hmm," said Everly. She put her hands in her lap and listened.

Then she tried a new game. She waited for the big notes. Boom, boom, boom. Each big note got one clap. Clap. Clap. Clap. Now her hands fit the song. "The claps go slow because the song goes slow," Everly said. Grandma smiled and clapped too.

Then Everly took a breath. She wanted to sing the words all by herself. She closed her eyes and thought hard. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The words came out. "How I wonder what you are." She did not stop. She keep singing, word after word, all the way to the end. "Up above the world so high." The last line came out big and clear.

After the song, Grandma gave her a pretzel. Everly bit it. It was salty and warm. The lady on stage bowed, and Everly clapped slow and steady, one clap for each big note, all the way to the end.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story: Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He wanted to write his name all by himself. He held the pencil in his whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. The N looked like a wide squiggle. His friend Sam had a small hat on his head to look like a writer. Nathan looked at Miss Jo's hand. She held her pencil with two fingers, like a little bird beak. Nathan tried it. He picked up his pencil the same way. Now his hand could move! He drew a straight line down. Then another line. The letter N looked like a real N. "Why is it easy now?" Nathan asked. "Because my fingers can hold it like a bird beak," he said. Miss Jo smiled wide. His pencil did not sink in his grip. Nathan wrote N, A, T, H, A, N. Sam clapped for him.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Margot sat on the floor. The big game was on TV. Grandma sat in the big chair. Uncle Sam sat on the couch. The cat sat on the rug. The cat was too lazy to move.

The team ran fast. Everyone jumped up. "Hooray!" they shouted. Margot could not see the TV. Grandma's legs were in the way. Margot asked, "Why can't I see?" She answered herself. "Everyone is standing up!"

So Margot hurried to get her little chair. She climbed up on it. Now she was tall too. Now she could see the TV just fine.

The team scored again. Everyone jumped up again. Margot stood on her chair too. She could still see! "I can see, I can see!" she said.

Grandma smiled and held her hand. The cat went back to sleep.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Jordan planted a tiny seed in the school garden. He made a deep hole with his finger. He dropped the seed in and patted the soil. Every day he ran to the garden to look. Nothing came up. His friend Mia had little green leaves already.

Teacher Kim sat with the children in a circle. "Let us share our garden news," she said kindly. Jordan said, "My seed is asleep." Then he watched Mia water her pot. She gave it water every day. Jordan had not given his seed any water at all.

So Jordan filled a small blue can. He poured the water on his dirt, slow and gentle. He did it the next day too. On the third morning, a green tip poked up. Jordan clapped his hands. "The water helped my seed wake up!" he said.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Ethan had a library book. It was about a big brown dog. The dog liked to bark at the mail truck. Ethan loved that book. He read it every night.

Tonight was bedtime. Ethan held the book tight. "I want to keep it," he said. "It is mine."

Dad shook his head. "The book has to go back," he said. "Wednesday is the day. Other kids want to read about the dog too."

Ethan turned the pages. He opened the front cover. He saw words there. "What does this say?" he asked.

Dad read the words out loud. They said who borrowed the book before. Ethan turned to the last page. He saw words there too. Words could tell him things!

At the library, Ethan gave the book to a lady. She typed on her computer. The computer made a little beep.

Then Ethan found a long, long book about trucks. "Can I take this one home?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "And when Wednesday comes, we bring it back. That is why the beep tells us the day."

Ethan held the new book. He read it front to back, just like the dog book.

"The book went back," he said, "so the beep can stop. And now I have a truck book!"

At bedtime, Ethan turned page after page. The last page had a big red truck on it. "Goodnight, truck," Ethan whispered.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Isla wants to sing the counting song at school. But she does not know all the words yet.

At circle time, Miss Rosa sings, "One, two, three." The children clap. Isla claps too. Then the song goes on. "Four, five, six." Isla hears her friend Tom sing it. She hums the tune but her mouth stays quiet. She is scared she will say the wrong words.

At play time, Isla pretends she is a farmer. She counts her toy cows. "One, two," she says. Then she stops. Tom sits next to her. He counts the rest with her. "Three, four, five." The cows are far across the rug. They walk the cows back. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten cows in the barn!

The next day, Miss Rosa starts the song. Isla takes a big breath. She sings, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the words come out in the right order. The singing helped her remember.

Miss Rosa smiles. "Sing it again," she says. Isla sings, and Tom sings too.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Levi loved the dress-up corner at school. Today he wanted to be a chef. He put on the big white hat and the red apron. "I will cook soup!" he said.

But first he had to find his shoes. The class was going outside. Levi looked under the table. He found one shoe. He found one sock. Where was the other sock? The sock was wet! It had fallen in the water table. Levi laughed. "My sock went swimming!" he said.

Miss Kim was gentle with the wet sock. She helped him lift it out of the water. She gave him a dry sock from his bag. Levi pulled it on. It felt warm and soft on his toes. Then his shoes went on fast. He gave Miss Kim a big hug. "Dry socks make shoes happy," Levi said. Then he ran outside to play.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jack ran to the red slide at the park. A girl was already at the ladder. Her name was Mia. Jack stopped and waited.

"Can I go too?" he asked. Mia nodded. "You go first. Then me," she said. So Mia went down the slide. Then Jack had his turn. It was fast and fun. Then Mia had another turn. Then Jack did too. They took turns, one by one.

Then Jack saw a round ball under the bench. He picked it up. A small boy ran over. He looked sad. "That is my ball," the boy said. Jack gave it back. "You can play too," said the boy. So all three played catch in the soft green grass. Jack had a bite of his apple. He opened his mouth for one big bite. Then he chose to share his apple too. He cut it with his fingers into little pieces.

"Next time, you go first," Jack told the boy. The boy smiled big.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Beau sat on the big stage. His teacher gave him a drum. He wanted to play the loud part in the song. He hit the drum very hard. The sound was too big and mixed up, like a puzzle with lost pieces.

The teacher put a card on the floor. "Can you read this card?" she asked. It said, "Tap soft." Beau tapped soft. The drum made a small, round sound. It fit the song just right.

"That is true," Beau said. "I tap soft, and the sound is soft." He tapped soft all the way to the end. The other kids clapped. Beau looked down at his drumstick. He gave it a tiny kiss, like a goodnight. "Good drum," he whispered.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan sat in his car seat. The sun shone on his knee through the window. The knee got hot. Declan pulled his knee away. It felt better in the shade.

"Hot," said Declan. "The sun made it hot."

Mom smiled from the front seat. "Good thinking," she said. Declan tried again. He put his hand in the sun. It was hot too. He moved his hand into the shade. Now it was cool.

They stopped at the gas station. Declan wanted to look around. He held Mom's hand tight. His shoe did not slip on the wet floor. Near the pump there was a big sign with a flame on it. Declan pointed. "Hot," he said. "Do not touch."

"You are right," said Mom. They walked back to the car. The fresh air felt cool on Declan's face. He climbed into his seat all by himself.

"Big boy," said Mom. She buckled him in. Declan waved at the sun through the window. "You are hot," he said. "I sit in the shade." The car drove home. Declan smiled at his cool, shady knee.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Arlo put on his red shirt. Today was a big game in the backyard. His team was the Red Robots.

Arlo ran to kick the ball. The sun was in his eyes. He could not see the ball. He kicked and missed. "Why can't I see?" he asked. "The sun is too bright."

Dad blew the whistle. It was time for half. That means the teams switch sides. The Red Robots ran to the other end.

Arlo looked up. No sun in his eyes now! "Where did the sun go?" he asked. "It is still there. We just face the other way." Arlo kicked the ball. He saw it go in the goal. Hooray!

At snack time, Arlo got orange slices. He began to eat one. It was sweet and juicy. "We switched sides and the sun went away," said Arlo. "Switch sides, sun goes away. Switch sides, sun goes away."

He kicked the ball again. Goal!

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Levi's bear was cold. His bear had no blanket at all.

"I will play house," said Levi. He got a small towel. He wrapped the towel around bear. Bear was warm now. But bear was still hungry. Levi made a pretend cake from a block. He put the block on a little plate. "Here is cake, bear," he said. Bear could not eat. Bears are toys. They do not open their mouths. Levi thought hard.

"What if I eat for bear?" he asked. "Yes! I can pretend for him." So Levi made a pretend bite. "Crunchy," he said, laughing. Bear was fed. Then Levi remembered one more thing. Babies need songs at night. He sang a soft song to bear. He rocked him in his arms. Mom came in to watch.

"You take good care of bear," she said. "He is my baby," said Levi. He laid bear down. "Night night, baby bear."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Jack ran up the steps with a big smile. He held a small cage. Inside was a white bird. "My first pet!" Jack said. Mom put the cage on the table. "Let's give her a name," she said. Jack clapped his hands. "Snow!" he said.

Jack wanted Snow to play right away. He banged on the cage. "Come out, Snow!" he said. Snow jumped to the back of the cage. She hid in the corner. She did not eat her seeds. Jack asked, "Why won't she play?" Mom said, "Watch her."

Jack sat very still. He made his voice small and soft. Snow peeked out. She hopped down. She pecked at her seeds. One white feather fell to the cage floor. Jack picked it up. "Snow is not scared now," he said.

The next morning, Snow chirped loud at Jack. She begged for more seeds with her beak open. Jack laughed and filled her cup. Then he held the feather up to the window. "Look, Snow," he said. "You can see the whole sky!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milan loved the play kitchen at school. Yesterday he cooked a red soup with a wooden carrot. He wanted to cook again today. But when he got to the kitchen, Sam was there. Sam was cooking a big pot now.

"Can I cook too?" asked Milan.

"Not now," said Miss Ada. "You can cook later, after Sam."

Milan waited. He watched Sam stir. The sun made a bright spot on the floor. Milan put his coin in the waiting jar. Each waiting child put one coin in. Sam put in three coins yesterday. Three coins meant a long turn.

Milan put in one coin. One coin meant a short wait. He sat down and watched the bright sun spot. He counted to ten. Then Sam was done.

"Now?" asked Milan.

"Now," said Miss Ada.

Milan cooked his soup. He stirred and stirred. "Today I waited," he said. "Tomorrow I will bring more coins. More coins, more cooking."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson woke up in his warm bed. The sun was on his wall. He wanted his blue socks. He looked under the bed. One sock was there. One sock was not.

Jaxson looked in his toy box. No sock. He looked in the closet. No sock. Then he saw mud on the floor. Little muddy footprints. One, two, three steps. They went to the door.

Jaxson followed the prints. The girl next door was outside. Her name was Mia. She had his sock on her hand, like a puppet. "It fell out the window," she said. Jaxson laughed. The sock was dirty.

Mama put the sock in the wash. It spun around and around. Then it hung on the line. The wind made it dance. Jaxson counted his socks on the line. One, two. Now he had two clean socks again.

At bath time, Jaxson washed his feet well. He did not want dirty feet again. He put on his pajamas. They were soft and warm. He left one sock out for Mia. "For your puppet hand," he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zoe and her family drove to a big park. Their car had four wheels. The wheels went round and round. Zoe held her juice box.

The car turned. The juice tipped. "It fell because the car turned," said Zoe. Daddy laughed. "That's right," he said. "I will go slow now."

Then Zoe looked in her lap. Her teddy was not there. She looked on the floor. No teddy. Her eyes got big. "I want teddy," she said.

Mommy reached back. She opened the big bag. She opened the little bag too. Then she held up teddy. "Teddy was packed away," said Mommy. "We brought him from home."

Zoe hugged teddy tight. She gave him a sip spot on her lap. An ugly bug walked by the window. Zoe did not mind it now.

The car stopped. Daddy opened the door. Trees and birds were everywhere. Zoe held Mommy's hand and stepped out.

"Home is far, but teddy is here," said Zoe.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Charlie went to the basketball court with her dad. She had a red beanbag and one big blue ball. "I want to get the beanbag in the hoop," she said. She threw it up. The beanbag hit the hoop and fell down.

Charlie tried again. She threw it far, far up. It went over the hoop. Then she threw it soft and low. It went under. She sat down on the long bench. "I will try one more time," she said. She looked at the hoop. She held the beanbag tight and threw it just over the front of the hoop. The beanbag went in! "One in the hoop," said Charlie. "One happy girl!"

Then Dad rolled the big blue ball to her. Charlie held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. "Ow," she said softly. Dad rolled it again. This time Charlie put out both hands. She pulled them in close to her chest. The ball stuck to her like a magnet! "I caught it!" she said. "Two hands catch the big ball. Two hands!"

Dad clapped. Charlie patted the ball like a good friend. "One beanbag, one ball, one hoop," she said. "Now I know just what to do."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Lincoln ran to the school garden. He had three little seeds in his hand. "Today we plant carrots!" he said.

His teacher gave him a cup of water. Lincoln poured it on the dirt. Then he pushed each seed down. He patted the soil on top. "Grow, grow, grow," he whispered.

The next day, Lincoln brought his lunch. He had salty soup in a thermos. He did not want the rest. "The plants can drink it," he said. He poured the salty soup on his dirt.

Two days later, his friend Maya yelled, "Look! My seed is up!" Lincoln looked at his dirt. Nothing was there. Tiny green leaves were not poking out. His seed was not growing. It was a puzzle. "Why is my seed not up?" he asked. He looked and looked.

Then Lincoln saw the wet spot. It smelled like soup. "Oh no. The soup was too salty," he said. "Salty water makes seeds not grow. Water is what they need." Maya nodded. "Plain water," she said.

Lincoln got the hose. He washed the salty soup away. He watered his spot with clean water. Every day he came back. On day four, he saw a fat pink worm crawl by. Then, right next to the worm, a tiny green tip pushed up out of the soil.

"My carrot is coming!" Lincoln shouted. He jumped up and down. Maya clapped. The worm wiggled back into the dirt.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was ready. Nora reached for a crunchy carrot.

"Stop," said Grandma. "First we wash hands. Soap takes twenty seconds."

Nora made a face. "That is too long!" Twenty seconds felt big to her.

"We can sing while we wash," said Grandma. "The happy song, all the way through."

Grandma turned on the water. She made soap bubbles on Nora's hands. They sang together. Nora rubbed and rubbed. The song ended. The water turned gray. The bubbles slid down the drain.

Nora looked at the water. "The dirt went away," she said. "The soap pushed it off!"

"Yes," said Grandma. "That is the answer."

Nora marched to the table with clean hands. She took a big bite of the carrot. It went crunch.

After lunch, Nora used the toilet. Then she ran to Grandma. "Soap time!" she said. "Twenty seconds, all by myself."

Grandma smiled and helped her reach the soap.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Emmett woke up from his nap. He smelled something sweet. "Cookies!" he said. But where were they?

He used his eyes to look. He saw a big bowl on the table. He saw flour on the floor. Mom came in with a broom. She began to sweep the flour away. "You have a cookie nose," Mom laughed. "It sniffed them out!"

Emmett heard a click. His ears heard it! The click came from the oven. "Is that the oven, Mom?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "The oven is hot. Hot ovens make cookies bake."

One, two, three, four, five, Emmett counted. He counted his eyes. He counted his ears. He counted his nose. "That is three helpers," he said. "My nose helped most today. My nose found the cookies!" Mom laughed so hard her hair went wild.

Then the timer rang. Ding! Emmett touched the cookie with one little finger. It was warm. He took a bite. Yum! Sweet and gooey. "My tongue likes cookies best," he said. "My tongue wins!"

Mom handed him milk. Emmett held up his cookie and said, "Best nose day ever." Then he took another big bite.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Riley was at Grandma's house. She wanted a snack. "Count ten crackers," said Grandma. "Then you can eat them." Riley began to count. "One, two, three." Then she stopped. What came next? She could not remember.

Grandma hummed a counting song while she folded a blanket. "One, two, three, four, five," sang Grandma. The kitchen was quiet, so Riley heard every word. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Grandma. Riley clapped. The song had shown her the next words!

Riley counted again, like a song. "One, two, three, four, five. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten crackers sat on the plate. But the tenth cracker looked funny. It had little ears! "Grandma, a cracker has ears!" Grandma laughed. It was a dry piece of bread shaped like a bunny. Riley took a big bite of the bunny cracker anyway. "Ten tastes better," she said.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah was at the beach with her mom. There was a little pool next to the sand. Leah wanted to swim in it. She held the wall and kicked her legs. But when she let go, she sank down fast.

Then Leah watched a big girl in the pool. The girl put her face in the water. She blew little bubbles out of her mouth. Leah tried it too. She put her face in and blew bubbles. Her body popped up like a ball! "Why do I float now?" Leah asked. Mom smiled. "Because you let your air out slow," she said. Leah blew more bubbles and floated all the way to the steps.

After the pool, they went to bathe in the warm sea. Leah washed off the sand. Then they sat on a towel and ate a big piece of cake. Some sand got on it. "It's crunchy," Leah said with a giggle. Mom laughed and gave her a new piece. Leah ate it all up and looked at the pool. "Bubbles tomorrow," she said.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Hazel stood in the backyard with her dragon. The dragon was green and small. He was a toy, not an animal. But Hazel pretended he was real.

"Dragon, you must be hungry," she said. She ran inside and got a cracker. Crackers are food. Real things eat food. She held the cracker up to the dragon's mouth. The cracker just sat there. It did not get smaller. The dragon did not eat.

Then she heard a sound behind her. It was a small bark. Her dog Biscuit ran up on four straight legs. He sniffed the cracker. He ate it in one bite. Biscuit was an animal, and animals eat food.

"So that is why," said Hazel. "Biscuit is real. Dragons are pretend." She patted Biscutt on his head. Then she held her dragon up high and whispered, "You can eat pretend crackers." She picked up a little stone and set it near the dragon's mouth. "There," she said. "All gone, little dragon."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood still in the kitchen. "Why is it dark?" he asked. "The power went out," said Mama. "No power means no lights."

Mama found the flashlight. She clicked it on. A big circle of light fell on the floor. Jules made his hands into a shape in the light. The shape looked like a bunny. Jules watered his little plant by the window, and the light helped him see the pot.

Jules wanted cold milk. He went to the fridge. "Can I leave the door open?" he asked. "No," said Mama. "The cold will run away." Jules closed the door fast. He waited. The fridge stayed cold inside because the door was shut.

Later, the lights came back on. The lamp glowed warm and yellow. "The power came back!" said Jules. "That is true," said Mama. She smiled. Jules looked at his bunny shape on the wall. It was gone now. But he could still see the little plant by the window. Its green leaf was standing up tall. Jules gave the leaf one soft pat. "Goodnight, plant," he said.
